claims.text: The untreated refractory high-entropy alloy has a predominantly homogeneous single-phase microstructure.
The untreated alloy has excellent strength but limited ductility and nonuniform deformation.
Adding 1–3 at.% Zr and applying controlled annealing will induce fine, uniformly dispersed B2 intermetallic precipitates.
The induced B2 precipitates will be ductile.
The precipitates will form both at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
The nanoscale B2 precipitates will enable more homogeneous deformation by modifying grain-boundary and intragranular microstructure.
Zirconium addition lowers the nucleation barrier for the B2 phase.
An optimal precipitate size and distribution will delay strain localization and distribute deformation more uniformly.
Delayed strain localization and more uniform deformation will increase ductility.
The B2 precipitates will act as energy-absorbing features during impact.
The precipitates will preserve impact-induced energy-release performance without significantly compromising the high-strength refractory matrix.
The treatment will increase elongation to failure by approximately 20–30% relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will reduce yield or ultimate strength by less than 10% relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will retain impact-induced energy-release capability relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will be effective at ambient and moderately elevated temperatures.
The treatment will be effective under both quasi-static tensile loading and dynamic impact loading.
The beneficial effect requires the Zr concentration to remain within approximately 1–3 at.%.
Departures from the proposed Zr range or annealing conditions may prevent the desired precipitate distribution or cause excessive softening.
Established microalloying and precipitation-strengthening principles support the expected qualitative ductility improvement.
